abstract: Liver fibrosis is a common progressive liver disease that can cause liver dysfunction and lead to serious complications. Zi Qi decoction (ZQ) is a traditional formulation that exerts pharmacological effects on the treatment of liver fibrosis. However, precise intervention mechanisms remain unclear. The aim of this study was to synergistically harness proteomics and metabolomics techniques to elucidate the specific target of ZQ and its potential mechanism of action. A carbon tetrachloride (CCl 4 )-induced liver fibrosis mouse model was established. Subsequently, the protective effect of ZQ on liver fibrosis mice was evaluated according to histopathological examination and biochemical indicators. Quantitative proteomics based on data independent acquisition (DIA) and non-targeted metabolomic analyses revealed the pharmacodynamic mechanism of ZQ. In addition, various cellular and molecular assays were used to detect changes in glycolysis levels in LSECs and mouse liver fibrosis models. The study results showed that ZQ significantly alleviated CCl 4 -induced liver injury and fibrosis in mice. DIA-based quantitative proteomics and non-targeted metabolomics analyses indicated that ZQ treatment downregulated glycolysis-related proteins such as PKM2, PFKP, and HK2, while regulating glycolysis-related metabolites and pathways. In addition, ZQ down-regulated glycolytic activity in mice with liver fibrosis and in LSECs, and inhibited CXCL1 secretion and neutrophil recruitment. ZQ inhibited LSEC glycolysis and mitigated neutrophil infiltration, thereby playing a therapeutic role in liver fibrosis. Materials and methods
Animals and model establishment
Thirty six-week-old male C57BL/6 mice (weighting 18–22 g) purchased from Zhejiang Academyof Medical Sciences (certificate No.: SCXK[Zhe]2019-0004) were raised in an environmentally controlled room (20–26 °C, 12 h alternating light/dark cycle) at Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine (Nanjing, China). Animal welfare was performed according to the National Institutes of Health guidelines and regulations. They were randomly divided into two groups after one week of being adaptively fed: the control group (
n
= 6) and the CCl
4
group (
n
= 24). Mice were intraperitoneally injected with 0.5mL/kg body weight CCl
4
(10% v/v in olive oil) thrice a week for 12 weeks to successfully establish CCl
4
-induced liver fibrosis mouse models. From the beginning of the 9th week, all the mice in the CCl
4
group were randomly divided into four groups: Model, ZQ-Low, ZQ-Middle, and ZQ-High groups, each consisting of 6 individuals. Mice in the ZQ-Low, ZQ-Middle, and ZQ-High groups received daily intragastric gavage with ZQ (8.8 g/kg, 17.6 g/kg, 35.2 g/kg body weight, respectively). All animals were euthanized via cervical dislocation at the end of the experiment, and blood and liver samples were collected for further analysis.
ZQ preparation
The ZQ consists of 9 herbs including Radix Arnebiae, Paeonia suffruticosa Andr, Paeonia lactiflora Pall, Rehmannia glutinosa Libosch, Panax notoginseng, Atractylodes Lancea, Phellodendron amurense, Radix Sophorae Fiavescentis, and Sedum sarmentosum Bunge
14
. These granules of TCM were purchased from Jiangyin Tianjiang Pharmaceutical Co. (Jiangyin, China). They were all subjected to strict quality control measures. A previously established method was used for the preparation process
14
.
Serum biochemical analysis
Levels of aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), and alkaline phosphatase (ALP)were determined using an automatic biochemical analyser (Hitachi, Tokyo, Japan).
Liver histopathology detection
Liver tissue was fixed using 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) and then embedded in paraffin. The specimens were sectioned at 4 μm and stained with haematoxylin and eosin (H&E), Masson, and Sirius Red. The light microscope (Leica Microsystems, Wetzlar, Germany) was used to capture photographs of the stained sections in random fields.
CXCL1 ELISA detection
The levels of CXCL1 released in the culture medium were determined using an ELISA kit (Enzyme-linked Biotechnology Co, Ltd. Shanghai, China) following the manufacturer’s guidelines.
Proteomic analysis and data acquisition
Protein extraction, quantification, reduction, alkylation, enzymatic digestion into peptide fragments, and peptide desalting were performed as sample preprocessing steps for each liver tissue sample. Subsequently, liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) data acquisition based on the data-independent acquisition (DIA) technique was performed by EASY MS Biotechnology (Nanjing, China) to measure protein expression in the liver tissue. Liquid chromatography/tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis was performed using a NanoElute liquid chromatography system (Bruker Daltonics Inc., Billerica, MA, USA) and a hybrid TIMS quadrupole time of flight (TOF) mass spectrometer (Bruker TimsTOF Pro). Direct DIA was used for mass spectrometry data acquisition to obtain qualitative and quantitative protein results. The collected raw MS files were analysed using DIA-NN software based on the
Mus musculus
UniProt database (
https://www.uniprot.org/
) (UniProt-Mus musculus-10090-2019-10) for protein identification and quantification. Proteins with over 60% quantitative information were selected for further analysis, and missing values were imputed using the k-nearest neighbours (KNN) algorithm method. Data were normalised using the median value method to correct for sample loading differences, followed by a log2 transformation. Single-factor analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed using R language (version 4.0.2), and Tukey’s test was used to compare differences between two groups. Fold Change (FC) quantifies relative change between data sets. FC > 1.5 or < 0.667, and
P
< 0.05 were set as the criteria for significant changes between any of the two groups. Subsequently, bioinformatics analyses including principal component analysis (PCA), volcano plot analysis, Gene Ontology (GO) annotation enrichment analysis, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) annotation enrichment analysis, and functional enrichment analysis were performed to explore the mechanism of ZQ treatment on liver fibrosis based on the Metascape website (
https://metascape.org
) .
Metabolomics analysis and data acquisition
Liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) was performed using an EASY MS Biotechnology. A 50 µL of serum sample was placed in a 1.5 mL Eppendorf tube, and 200 µL of cold methanol (containing internal standard) was added. The mixture was vortexed for 1 min and incubated at room temperature for 10 min. Subsequently, the mixture was centrifuged at 14,000 ×
g
for 15 min at 4 °C, and 200 µL of the supernatant was transferred to a new 1.5 mL Eppendorf tube. The supernatant was freeze-dried and stored at -20 °C for further use. The freeze-dried serum extract was reconstituted in 100 µL of 20% methanol/water solution prior to injection analysis. All samples were analysed using a Q-Exactive high-resolution mass spectrometry system (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) coupled with a ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography (UPLC) system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) to obtain qualitative and quantitative results. All data were collected using Xcalibur software (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and subjected to peak matching and qualitative metabolite analysis using MS-DIAL software. Finally, a peak table containing metabolite retention time, m/z, and peak area was exported. Metabolites were identified and analysed using MS-DIAL software. Subsequently, quantitative data were corrected using internal standards (IS), and the curated data were uploaded to the MetaboAnalyst website. The data were pre-processed using a Pareto scaling algorithm. Principal component analysis and orthogonal partial least squares discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) were performed for all metabolites. OPLS-DA is employed to discern differences among two or more groups within high-dimensional datasets. Q2 serves as a metric to quantitatively assess the predictive prowess of the OPLS-DA model.Significance was assessed using the Tukey test to calculate P-values, variable importance in projection (VIP) scores were computed using the partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) dimensionality reduction method, and fold change was calculated to measure the impact and discriminative power of the metabolite component contents on sample classification. The VIP is utilized for evaluating the individual variable’s contribution to model prediction. A higher VIP score indicates a more substantial impact of the variable on sample classification within the model. Metabolites were selected as potential biomarkers when the criteria of P-value < 0.05, Fold Change (FC) > 1.5 or < 0.667, and VIP > 1 were met, indicating statistical significance.
Western blotting
Tissue or cellular proteins were extracted using a RIPA lysis buffer, subjected to sodium dodecyl sulphate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis, and transferred to nitrocellulose membranes. Primary antibodies against Hexokinase 2 (22029-1-AP; 1:500), PFKP (13389-1-AP;1:2000), PKM2 (15822-1-AP;1:1000), and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GADPH) (10494-1-AP; 1:5000) were used and incubated overnight at 4ºC. Then, the membranes were incubated with secondary antibodies for 1 h. After three additional washes with tris-buffered saline with tween (TBST), the blots were visualised using a chemiluminescence imager (Quantity One; Bio-Rad Laboratories Inc., Hercules, CA, USA).
10 RT-qPCR
Total RNA was extracted from LSEC or mouse liver tissues using TRIzol reagent. Subsequently, the extracted RNA was reverse transcribed into cDNA using a dedicated kit (Yeasen Biotech Co., Ltd.). RT-qPCR was performed using the SYBR Green Master Mix (Yeasen Biotech Co., Ltd). Ct values were normalized to beta-actin (β-actin). The primer sequences used in this study were as follows:
HK2, Forward primer: 5′-ATCAAAGAGAACAAGGGCGAGGAG-3′,
Reverse primer: 5′-GCGGAGGAAGCGGACATCAC-3′;
PFKP, Forward primer: 5′-CTGGCAAGGGAAGACAAGAACAAC-3′,
Reverse primer: 5′-GAGCCGCACAGGACCGTATG-3′;
PKM2, Forward primer: 5′-TGTGCCGCCTGGACATTGAC-3′,
Reverse primer: 5′-AATTCAGCCGAGCCACATTCATTC-3′;
β-actin, Forward primer: 5′-GATGGTGGGAATGGGTCAGAAGG-3′,
Reverse primer: 5′-TTGTAGAAGGTGTGGTGCCAGATC-3′.
Immunofluorescence assay
Thin Sect. (4 μm) of liver tissue were de-paraffinized using 5% BSA, and were then incubated overnight withanti-LYVE1(51011-1-AP, Proteintech Group, USA), anti-PFKFB3 (PA5-106274, Abcam, Cambridges, UK) at 4 °C. The next day, the sections were treated with the corresponding secondary antibody and DAPI reagents. Changes in fluorescence were monitored using an inverted fluorescence microscope (Leica Microsystems). The images were blindly acquired from randomly selected fields of view.
Immunohistochemistry
Liver tissue sections were dewaxed, immersed in 0.3% hydrogen peroxide to block endogenous peroxidase activity, and blocked with 5% BSA at room temperature for 30 min. The sections were washed with PBS, and incubated with anti-myeloperoxidase (MPO) (22225-1-AP, Proteintech Group, USA), anti-CXCL1 (12335-1-AP, Proteintech Group, USA) overnight at 4 °C. On the second day, after washing, the sections were incubated with horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated secondary antibody for 50 min. Diaminobenzidine (DAB) was used as the chromogen, followed by counterstaining with hematoxylin. Finally, fixed and stained slides were photographed using the microscope (Leica Microsystems).
Preparing drug-containing serum
In accordance with a method outlined in a previous study
14
, twenty healthy male SD rats were fed under normal conditions and randomly divided into Control group, ZQ-Low group, ZQ-Middle group, and ZQ-high group. Rats in the ZQ groups received ZQ (1 mL/100 g body weight) at doses of 2.75 g/kg, 5.5 g/kg, and 11 g/kg, respectively. Rats in the Control groups were given 0.9% normal saline once daily for 8 days. The blood was collected after the last gavage, and centrifuged to extract a supernatant.
Cell culture
Immortalized human sinusoidal endothelial cells (IM-H399) were procured from IMMOCELL (Xiamen, Fujian, China). The cells were maintained in complete endothelial cell medium supplemented with 10% foetal bovine serum (FBS) and 100 U/mL of streptomycin and penicillin, and cultured at 37 °C with 5% CO
2
. Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) (Chamot Biotechnology, Shanghai, China) was dissolved in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) at a concentration of 40 ng/mL to induce cell stimulation
17
,
18
.
Cell counting kit 8 (CCK8) assays
LSECs were plated in 96-well plates and allowed to incubate overnight at 37℃ under a 5% CO
2
atmosphere. After 24 h of treatment with different concentrations of ZQ, 10 µL of CCK8 reagent was added to each well. Cell viability was measured using OD at 450 nm.
Measurement of lactate
Lactate levels in LSEC and mouse liver tissue were assessed according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute, Nanjing, China).
Glucose oxidase (GOD) activity assays
Glucose consumption by LSEC was determined using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay kit (Shanghai Meilian Biology Technology Co. Ltd., Shanghai, China) to measure GOD activity according to the manufacturer’s protocols.
Enzyme activity assays
The intracellular activities of HK2, PFKP, and PKM2 in LSECs were measured according to the manufacturer’s protocols (Shanghai Meilian Biology Technology Co., Ltd.). MPO activity, a clear indicator of neutrophil accumulation, was detected using an MPO assay kit (Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute).
Data analysis
The non-proteomic data were analysed using GraphPad Prism 8.0 software. All data are presented as the mean ± standard deviation (SD), demonstrating conformity to a normal distribution and homogeneity of variance. Unpaired t-test was employed for pairwise comparisons, and the one-way ANOVA was utilized for multiple group comparisons. A p value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Introduction
Liver fibrosis is the pathological basis for the development of various chronic liver diseases. Persistent liver injury, such as chronic inflammation, promotes the aggravation of liver fibrosis to cirrhosis, which may lead to liver cancer or liver failure
1
,
2
. Statistics show that liver disease causes 2 million deaths annually, accounting for 4% of all deaths
3
. Most of these deaths are caused by complications arising from cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Therefore, liver fibrosis is a key factor contributing to the rise in liver disease mortality. Despite the high medical need, effective clinical drugs are lacking .
Chronic or excessive inflammatory responses are often accompanied by a series of metabolic abnormalities. To meet the energy needed for the inflammatory response, cells increase the production of ATP by increasing metabolic pathways such as glycolysis
4
,
5
. Studies have shown that endothelial cells (ECs) have higher rates of glycolysis than other healthy cell types
6
. 85% of ATP in ECs is produced glycolytically by converting glucose to lactate
7
. LSECs are unique types of vascular endothelial cells in the liver that are critical for maintaining the homeostasis of the liver microenvironment and keeping hepatic stellate cells (HSC) and Kupffer cells in a resting state, thereby preventing the progression of liver fibrosis. Recent studies have shown that increased glycolysis in LSECs can enhance CXCL1 expression by modifying nuclear pores and facilitating NF-kB translocation
8
. However, the inhibition of glycolysis in LSECs impedes CXCL1-mediated neutrophil infiltration and improves liver fibrosis
9
. Therefore, targeting LSEC glycolysis is a promising strategy for alleviating liver fibrosis.
In recent years, the benefit of using traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) to treat liver fibrosis has increasingly been emphasised
10
–
12
. ZQ is a traditional herbal formula widely used in clinical therapy for liver fibrosis. In our preliminary research, we proposed its potential pharmacological effects on liver fibrosis
13
. ZQ effectively inhibits the activation of hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) by suppressing the NF-κB and MAPK signalling pathways downstream of TLR4, thereby restraining the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6
14
. This intervention shows promise to ameliorate liver damage and inflammation, and ultimately alleviate liver fibrosis. However, the effects of ZQ on LSEC glycolysis during liver fibrosis remain unclear.
Determining the anti-liver fibrosis mechanisms of TCM presents a formidable challenge, primarily owing to the extensive and intricate array of active constituents inherent in TCM formulations
10
. The integration of cutting-edge methodologies, such as metabolomics and proteomics, has emerged as a promising avenue for precisely elucidating the effects of therapeutic agents on liver fibrosis at the molecular level
15
,
16
. The aim of this study was to synergistically harness proteomic and metabolomics techniques to elucidate the specific targets and underlying mechanisms of action of ZQ, thereby contributing new perspectives towards clinical interventions and therapeutic strategies for liver fibrosis.

Results
ZQ alleviates liver injury and fibrosis in CCl4-induced mice
A well-established mouse model of liver fibrosis induced by intraperitoneal injection of CCl
4
was used to evaluate the effect of ZQ on liver fibrosis. Markers of liver injury, including serum ALT, AST, ALP, and TBIL, and markers of liver fibrosis, including serum PC-III, LN, and HA significantly increased in the model group. However, treatment withdifferent concentrations of ZQ (low at 8.8 g/kg/d, middle at 17.6 g/kg/d, and high at 35.2 g/kg/d) effectively counteracted the increased levels of these markers caused by CCl4, with the middle dose of ZQ demonstrating particular efficacy Fig.
1
A and B). The histopathological examination using H&Estaining demonstrated extensive inflammatory cell infiltration in the model group. However, ZQ treatment led to a reduction in liver inflammation (Fig.
1
C). Furthermore, Sirius Red and Masson staining showed that collagen deposition was remarkably attenuated using ZQ treatment, compared to the Model group. Collectively, these findings demonstrated the efficacy of ZQ in mitigating CCl
4
-induced liver injury and fibrotic alterations in mice.

ZQ inhibits glycolysis of CCl4-induced liver fibrosis in mice
To further explore the impact of ZQ on the glycolytic pathway in mice with liver fibrosis, we selected key glycolysis-related proteins, such as HK2, PFKP, and PKM2, for validation based on the changes observed through FCM clustering and relevant literature. Our proteomic data indicated that the expression levels of HK2, PFKP, and PKM2 initially increased in the model group, but decreased after ZQtreatment (Fig.
4
A). Subsequently, we evaluated the effect of ZQ on mRNA and protein expression of HK2, PFKP and PKM2 in mice using RT-qPCR and western blot analysis. Consistent with proteomics results, the expression of these proteins increased in the model group and decreased significantly after ZQ treatment. (Fig.
4
B and C). Lactate production is a critical step in glycolysis, and we assessed the liver lactate levels in mice using colorimetry. The results suggested that lactate levels in mice with liver fibrosis were significantly reduced after ZQ treatment (Fig.
4
D). Collectively, these findings indicate that ZQ may play a role in inhibiting glycolytic metabolism in mice with liver fibrosis.

ZQ suppresses the glycolysis in LSEC
Glycolysis is a crucial pathway for cells to obtain energy, vital for maintaining normal cellular functions and metabolic activities. 37566009As a major component of hepatic non-parenchymal cells, LSECs participate in preserving the homeostasis of intrahepatic microcirculation. During liver fibrosis, LSECs may adapt to and respond to changes in the microenvironment by modulating their glycolytic pathways
18
. The glycolytic enzyme PFKFB3 is highly expressed in ECs and is regarded as a target for inhibiting endothelial glycolysis
6
. By immunofluorescence co-staining, we observed a significant correlation between PFKFB3 and LYVE1 (indicator LSEC) in the model group. However, the abundance of PFKFB3 was reduced in LSECs of ZQ-treated mice (Fig.
6
A). This result suggests that ZQ may inhibit the progression of liver fibrosis by regulating LSEC glycolysis. Therefore, we further investigated the regulatory mechanisms of ZQ in LSEC glycolysis in vitro. We used CCK8 assay to determine the effect of different concentrations of serum containing ZQ on the viability of LSECs(Fig.
6
B).It is demonstrated that when the concentrations of serum containing ZQ reached 20%, the cell viability decreased significantly. Therefore, we selected a maximum concentration of 15% for subsequent experiments. LSECs were stimulated with VEGF (40 ng/mL), with or without ZQ. The results showed that ZQ reduced glucose consumption and lactate levels in LSECs in a concentration-dependent manner (Fig.
6
C and D). ZQ also decreased the intracellular protein expression and activity of key glycolytic enzymes HK2, PFKP, and PKM2(Fig.
6
E and F). These results indicate that ZQ can effectively inhibit LSEC glycolysis.

ZQ attenuates the CXCL1 secretion and neutrophil infiltration
Recently, it has been reported that LSEC glycolysis can induce the production of neutrophil chemoattractant CXCL1 in LSEC, thereby recruiting neutrophils to generate NETs and promote liver fibrosis
24
. KEGG enrichment analyses showed that down-regulated DEPs after ZQ treatment was associated with neutrophil chemotaxis (Fig.
3
A). Furthermore, Gene Ontology Biological Process (GOBP) analysis highlights the involvement of these DEPs in pivotal biological processes, including phagocytosis, leukocyte migration, regulation of actin cytoskeleton organization, and lymphocyte proliferation(Fig.
S2
A-C). These processes are closely associated with the inflammatory response and immune modulation. Notably, the participation of leukocyte migration and phagocytic processes aligns with the pivotal role of neutrophil infiltration in the inflammatory cascade.Therefore, we further investigated the effect of ZQ on LSECs-derived CXCL1 and neutrophil recruitment.
We first evaluated the effect of ZQ on the expression ofCXCL1 both in vivo and in vitro. Immunohistochemical results showed that the expression level of CXCL1 in liver tissues of the model group was significantly higher than that of the control group, but reduced after ZQ treatment. (Fig.
7
A). Consistent with the vivo results, the CXCL1 level released into the culture medium was decreased by ZQ (Fig.
7
B). Myeloperoxidase (MPO) plays an important regulatory role in the migration and recruitment of neutrophils, thereby inhibiting neutrophil infiltration in tissues
25
,
26
. Immunohistochemistry detection revealed that compared with the model group, the MPO level in liver tissue was significantly down-regulated after ZQ treatment(Fig.
7
C). Subsequently, we further examined MPO activity using the kit assay, and obtained the same results (Fig.
7
D). These observations suggest that ZQ effectively inhibits the secretion CXCL1 and neutrophil infiltration.

Discussion
Organ fibrosis indicates the progress of chronic inflammatory diseases, which account for 45% of all deaths worldwide
27
. Liver fibrosis development directly affects chronic liver disease prognosis and raises cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma risks
28
,
29
. Therefore, anti-liver fibrosis therapies need to be developed urgently.
Research shows that drugs modulating multiple core signalling components or targeting multiple pathways are generally more promising than those affecting only a small part of the complex network involved
30
,
31
. ZQ is an empirical decoction created by the TCM scientist Zhou Zhongying, with complex components and multi-target effects
14
. In this study, we demonstrated the efficacy of ZQ in alleviating liver damage and fibrosis in CCl
4
-induced liver fibrosis mice. DIA-based quantitative proteomic and untargeted metabolomics analyses were used to elucidate the potential pharmacological mechanisms by which ZQ alleviates liver fibrosis. Proteomic analysis revealed 930 DEPs after ZQ treatment, comprising 499 upregulated and 431 downregulated proteins (Fig.
2
C and D). KEGG analysis revealed that the downregulated DEPs were significantly enriched in signalling pathways related to glycolysis (Fig.
3
A). GOMF analysis illuminated the diverse biochemical activities of these DEPs, such asenzyme activator and phosphatase binding suggest potential regulatory roles in metabolic pathways, including glycolysis.Additionally, as delineated by the Metascape platformanalysis, we obtained similar results (Figure
S2
C).To gain further insights into the metabolic processes affected by ZQ, we performed metabolomics analysis. It revealed that ZQ influenced the levels of metabolites such as 1-methyladenosine, L-Glutamine, L-Pyroglutamic acid, and Uridine diphosphate-N-acetylglucosamine (Fig.
5
G). The unique roles of each of these metabolites in the glycolytic pathway ensure its proper functioning. For instance, 1-methyladenosine is involved in adenosine metabolism, which is closely linked to energy production
32
. L-Glutamine, an amino acid, acts as a carbon and nitrogen source for glycolysis, while L-Pyroglutamic acid and Uridine diphosphate-N-acetylglucosamine contribute to the synthesis of glycogen
21
,
33
. Liver fibrosis is a process with high energy requirements
34
. The reprogramming of metabolism has been identified as a potential target for anti-liver fibrosis therapy
35
, with glycolysis playing a pivotal role in this process
36
. Therefore, we focused on the effect of ZQ on glycolytic metabolism in the process of liver fibrosis. The results showed that ZQ could effectively reduce the expression level of glycolytic products and enzymes. This finding provides direct evidence that the therapeutic effect of ZQ is related to its ability to regulate abnormal liver glycolysis.
In recent years, growing attention has been paid to endothelial cells (ECs) metabolism, which prefers to rely on glycolysis for ATP production to support their functionality rather than oxidative phosphorylation
37
. LSEC is a highly specialized endothelial cell in the liver, and LSEC glycolysis has been reported to play an important regulatory role in the process of liver fibrosis
18
,
38
. Our experimental findings further substantiate this view by revealing a conspicuous increase in intracellular glycolytic activity within LSECs in a mouse model of liver fibrosis (Fig.
6
A). Simultaneously, ZQ treatment effectively attenuated the expression and activityof glycolysis-related enzymes, including HK2, PFKP, and PKM2, and regulated the glucose consumption and lactate level in LSEC(Fig.
6
C-F). This prompted our focus to shift to the therapeutic implications of ZQ in regulating LSEC glycolysis during liver fibrosis.
Interestingly, recent studies have demonstrated that inhibition of LSEC glycolysis can reduce neutrophil infiltration, thus alleviating inflammation and liver fibrosis
18
.The LSECS-derived neutrophil chemoattractant CXCL1 plays an important role in this process. In addition, our proteomics results also elucidated the strong correlation between ZQ and neutrophils in liver fibrosis(Fig.
3
A and Figure
S2
). Therefore, inhibition of CXCL1 release and neutrophil recruitment induced by LSEC glycolysis, thereby reducing liver injury caused by neutrophil infiltration, may be a potential target for ZQ intervention in liver fibrosis. Our in vivo and in vitro experiments provided compelling evidence for the ability of ZQ to effectively inhibit CXCL1 secretion(Fig.
7
A and B). To further validate the role of ZQ in restraining neutrophil infiltration in liver fibrosis, we conducted experiments using myeloperoxidase (MPO), a marker of neutrophil infiltration and activation
39
. Our results showed that ZQ treatment reduced MPO levels and activity in the liver, which validated the effectiveness of ZQ in restraining neutrophil infiltration in liver fibrosis (Fig.
7
C and D).
Conclusion
In conclusion, our findings suggest that ZQ could potentially modulate LSEC glycolysis and subsequently inhibit neutrophil infiltration in liver fibrosis. By targeting LSEC glycolysis, ZQ may provide a novel therapeutic approach for the treatment of liver fibrosis(Fig.
8
). Future research will aim to elucidate the specific active ingredients within ZQ and further investigate its therapeutic potential in preclinical and clinical settings.
